stem: Ada needs a list of every PNG file under `/srv/assets`, including the files in its subdirectories. Which command does this?

options.rationale: find searches the directory tree below `/srv/assets`, and `-name` matches the file name against the quoted pattern.
The shell expands `*.png` in the current directory, not under `/srv/assets`, and ls doesn’t descend into subdirectories without `-R`.
grep searches the contents of files for the text "png", not their names.
find takes the starting directories first and the tests after them; here `*.png` is treated as a starting point, not a name test.

explanation: To search by file name through a whole directory tree, give find the starting directory and a `-name` test. Quote the pattern so the shell passes it to find instead of expanding it in the current directory.

stem: What is the difference between `/` and `/root` on a Linux system?

options.text: `/` is the administrator’s home directory, and `/root` is the top of the tree
options.rationale: The roles are the wrong way round.

options.text: Both names refer to the same directory, and `/root` is just a longer spelling
options.rationale: They are different directories.

options.text: `/` is the top of the whole file tree, and `/root` is the administrator’s home directory
options.rationale: `/` is the root directory, the start of every absolute path.

options.text: `/` is the home directory of the current user, and `/root` is a copy of it
options.rationale: The current user’s home is `~`, and `/root` isn’t a copy.

explanation: The root directory `/` contains everything else. `/root` is where the user `root` keeps personal files, just as `/home/mira` is Mira’s home.

stem: Jonas types `echo ~` in his terminal. What does the shell print?

options.rationale: The shell replaces a leading `~` with the current user’s home directory.
Bash expands an unquoted tilde before `echo` sees it.
`~` leads to the user’s own directory, not just its parent.
That is the administrator’s home, not Jonas’s.

explanation: `~` is a shell shortcut for the home directory of the current user, and `~name` means the home directory of another user. Quotes switch the expansion off.

stem: On a typical Linux system, where do ordinary users keep their personal files and settings?

options.text: In a directory below `/usr`, named after the user
options.rationale: `/usr` holds programs and shared data.

options.text: In a directory below `/etc`, named after the user
options.rationale: `/etc` holds system configuration.

options.text: In a directory below `/var`, named after the user
options.rationale: `/var` holds variable data such as logs and caches.

options.text: In a directory below `/home`, named after the user
options.rationale: For example `/home/ada` for the user ada.

explanation: Each user has a home directory, usually `/home/NAME`. `cd` with no argument and `cd ~` both lead there.

stem: Which of these is an absolute path?

options.rationale: It has no leading slash, so it starts in the current directory.
It starts at the root directory `/`.
It begins at the parent of the current directory.
It begins at the current directory.

explanation: An absolute path starts with `/` and means the same thing wherever you are. Anything else is relative to the current directory.

stem: Mira is in `/home/mira/projects/website`. Which relative path leads to `/home/mira/projects/pixel-raiders`?

options.rationale: This would be a directory inside `website`.
One level up gets to `projects`, and then `pixel-raiders` is inside it.
Two levels up lands in `/home/mira`, where there is no such directory.
The leading slash makes it an absolute path under the root directory.

explanation: `..` is the parent directory. From `website`, `..` is `projects`, so `../pixel-raiders` is its sibling.

stem: What do the special names `.` and `..` stand for in a directory?

options.text: The hidden files and the backup files in it
options.rationale: Hidden files merely begin with a dot.

options.text: The first and the last file in it
options.rationale: The names have nothing to do with the order of files.

options.text: The home directory and the root directory
options.rationale: Those are `~` and `/`.

options.text: The directory itself and its parent directory
options.rationale: Every directory has these two entries.

explanation: `.` is the current directory and `..` is the one above it. They appear in `ls -a`, but not in `ls -A`.

stem: What makes a file or directory hidden on Linux?

options.text: Its name begins with a dot
options.rationale: A plain `ls` skips every name that starts with `.`.

options.text: It has the hidden attribute set with `chmod`
options.rationale: `chmod` changes permissions, not visibility.

options.text: Its name ends with a tilde, like `notes.txt~`
options.rationale: The tilde usually marks a backup file, which is shown normally.

options.text: It is stored below a directory named `hidden`
options.rationale: No special directory name hides anything.

explanation: Hiding is just a naming convention: a leading dot. To hide a file, rename it with a dot in front; to see hidden entries, use `ls -a` or `ls -A`.

stem: Which command lists hidden entries, but leaves out the special entries `.` and `..`?

options.rationale: This is the long form of `-a`, which includes `.` and `..` too.
This lists directories themselves instead of their contents.
The capital A means “almost all”.
This asks for human-readable sizes in long listings.

explanation: `-a` shows every entry, including `.` and `..`. `-A` shows every entry except those two, which is usually what you want.

stem: Ada wants a listing with one line per file showing permissions, owner, size and modification date. Which option gives that?

options.rationale: This prints the names as one comma-separated list, with no details.
This shows the allocated size next to each name, nothing more.
The long format shows these details.
This prints one name per line without any details.

explanation: `-l` selects the long format. Combine it with `-a` for hidden files, and with `-h` for sizes like `4.0K`.

stem: Which command lists a directory and every directory below it, one block per directory?

options.rationale: The capital R makes the listing recursive.
This is the long form of `-r`, which only reverses the sort order.
This lists the directory itself instead of its contents.
This adds hidden entries but doesn’t descend.

explanation: `ls -R` is recursive. Be careful with the case: `ls -R` descends, while `cp -r` and `rm -r` use a lowercase r for the same idea.

stem: What does `cd` do when it is typed without any argument?

options.text: It stays where it is and prints the current directory
options.rationale: `pwd` is the command that prints the current directory.

options.text: It changes to the root directory `/`
options.rationale: The root directory needs `cd /`.

options.text: It changes back to the previous directory
options.rationale: That is `cd -`.

options.text: It changes to the user’s home directory
options.rationale: With no argument, `cd` goes home.

explanation: `cd` and `cd ~` both lead to the home directory, whichever directory you are in. `cd -` returns to the previous directory.

stem: Mira changed from her home directory to `/var/log` and now wants to jump straight back. Which command takes her to the directory she was in before?

options.rationale: This only moves to the parent, `/var`.
A lone dash stands for the previous directory.
This climbs two levels up, to `/`, which is not where she was.
This leads to `/home`, not to her own home directory.

explanation: Bash remembers the previous directory. `cd -` switches to it and prints its name.

stem: Jonas wants `find` to match file names ignoring upper and lower case, so that `README.md` and `readme.txt` are both found. Which test does this?

options.rationale: `-name` is case-sensitive and would miss `README.md`.
`-iname` works like `-name` but ignores case.
`-type` tests for the kind of entry, such as file or directory.
There is no such test in `find`.

explanation: `-name` compares names exactly; `-iname` ignores case. Quote the pattern so the shell passes the `*` to `find`.

stem: Ada needs the directories named `docs` under her home, and no ordinary files with that name. Which command does this?

options.rationale: `-type f` limits the results to ordinary files.
`-type` needs a value, such as `d`.
`ls` lists contents; it doesn’t search by name.
`-type d` limits the results to directories.

explanation: `find` combines tests: `-type d` keeps directories and `-name docs` keeps the matching names. Both must hold.

stem: Which of these names are hidden, so that a plain `ls` does not show them? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: It begins with a dot.
A hidden directory, since it begins with a dot.
Without the dot it’s an ordinary name.
The tilde at the end doesn’t hide anything.
An underscore is an ordinary character.

explanation: Only a leading dot hides a name, for files and directories alike. `ls -a` shows them.

stem: Which `ls` options include hidden entries in the listing? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: It lists all entries, including `.` and `..`.
The long form of `-A`: hidden entries, but not `.` and `..`.
The long format shows details, but no hidden files by itself.
It descends into directories, but still skips hidden names.
It lists directories themselves, not hidden ones.

explanation: Hidden entries show up with `-a` (`--all`) or `-A` (`--almost-all`). The other options change the format or the depth of the listing.

stem: Which of these are absolute paths? (Choose THREE.)

options.rationale: Starts with `/`.
Starts with `/`.
The root directory itself is an absolute path.
Starts at the parent of the current directory.
Starts in the current directory.
Starts in the current directory.

explanation: Any path that begins with `/` is absolute. Paths starting with a name, `.` or `..` depend on the current directory.

stem: Which commands list the PNG files in `/srv/assets` and in all of its subdirectories? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: `find` walks the whole tree below the start directory.
The extra test only drops directories that happen to end in `.png`.
The wildcard matches only the top directory, not the subdirectories.
The start directory must come first.
This lists only the directory itself.

explanation: `find START TESTS` searches the whole tree. A shell wildcard such as `*.png` only matches inside one directory, and the starting point has to come before the tests.

stem: Type the `ls` command that prints a long listing of the current directory including hidden entries.
explanation: `-l` gives the long format and `-a` adds the hidden entries. Short options can be combined in either order.

stem: Type the command that takes you back to your home directory from anywhere, using no path or only the shortcut for it.
explanation: Plain `cd` and `cd ~` both lead home.

stem: Type the command that moves up one level, to the parent of the current directory.
explanation: `..` is the parent directory, so `cd ..` goes up one level.

stem: Complete the command so that it lists `projects` and everything below it.
explanation: `-R` is the recursive option of `ls`; it needs the capital letter.

stem: Complete the command so that it finds every file named exactly `index.html` below `projects`.
explanation: `-name` compares the file name against a pattern; a plain name matches exactly that name.

stem: Type the command that prints the absolute path of the directory you are in.
explanation: `pwd` (print working directory) always prints an absolute path.

stem: Mira moves around the Pixel Raiders project. What does this command print?

options.rationale: `..` leaves `src`, and `docs` is the sibling directory in `pixel-raiders`.
`..` first goes up, so `docs` isn’t searched inside `src`.
Two levels up would be needed for that.
`..` goes up only one level.

explanation: `cd ../docs` goes up one level to `pixel-raiders` and then down into `docs`. `pwd` prints the resulting absolute path.

stem: Ada lists the project folder, including hidden entries. What does this command print?

options.rationale: A plain `ls` would show this, without `.gitignore` or the dot entries.
The hidden file `.gitignore` is missing.
`-a` shows `.` and `..` and the hidden `.gitignore`, and the list is sorted ignoring the dots.
This is the output of `ls -A`; `-a` adds `.` and `..`.

explanation: `ls -a .` lists the current directory with all entries, including `.`, `..` and `.gitignore`. The sort order ignores the leading dot.

stem: Mira is in her home directory. Type what this command prints.
explanation: The first `ls` prints the name as it was given, the expanded absolute path. The second prints the relative name. Both refer to the same file.

stem: Type what this command prints.
explanation: The shell replaces `~` with the home directory of the current user, so `~/projects` becomes `/home/mira/projects`.

stem: Mira jumps back and forth. What does this command print?

options.rationale: `cd -` prints the directory it moves to, not the one it leaves.
After `cd -` she is back in her home, so `pwd` doesn’t print `website`.
`cd -` prints the directory it returns to, her home, and `pwd` prints the same.
She went into `website`, not `projects`, before going back.

explanation: `cd -` goes back to the previous directory and prints its path. Mira was in her home before she entered `website`.

stem: Type what this command prints (the paths are sorted).
explanation: `find` prints paths in the form of its starting point, here relative ones. `sort` puts them in a fixed order, since `find` lists directory entries in no particular order.

stem: What does this command print?

options.rationale: `-type d` keeps all directories, including the starting one and those nested deeper.
The starting directory itself and the subdirectories `docs` and `src` are missing.
`find` also prints the starting directory `projects`.
`-type d` leaves out ordinary files such as `README.md`.

explanation: `find` starts by testing the start directory itself, then everything below it. Only directories pass `-type d`.

stem: Type what this command prints (`-1` puts one entry on each line).
explanation: With `-F`, `ls` appends a `/` to each directory name. `-1` prints one entry per line instead of columns.

stem: Mira wants to see which release files are biggest. What does this command print?
output:
hero.png
theme.ogg
credits.txt
level10.txt
level2.txt
level1.txt

options.text:
level1.txt
level2.txt
level10.txt
credits.txt
theme.ogg
hero.png
options.rationale: That is the order of `ls -1Sr`, smallest first.

options.text:
credits.txt
hero.png
level1.txt
level10.txt
level2.txt
theme.ogg
options.rationale: That is plain alphabetical order, as `ls -1` prints it.

options.text:
hero.png
theme.ogg
credits.txt
level10.txt
level2.txt
level1.txt
options.rationale: Largest first, as `-S` does.

options.text:
theme.ogg
hero.png
credits.txt
level10.txt
level1.txt
level2.txt
options.rationale: That is the order of `ls -1X`, grouped by extension.

explanation: `-S` sorts by size, largest first, and `-1` puts one name on each line. `hero.png` is 30 bytes and `level1.txt` is 4.

stem: Ada lists the release folder grouped by file extension. Type what this command prints.
output:
theme.ogg
hero.png
credits.txt
level10.txt
level1.txt
level2.txt
explanation: `-X` sorts by extension: `.ogg`, then `.png`, then the three `.txt` files. Files with the same extension are sorted by name, and `level10.txt` comes before `level1.txt` because `0` sorts before `.`.

stem: Jonas wants the smallest file first. Type what this command prints.
output:
level1.txt
level2.txt
level10.txt
credits.txt
theme.ogg
hero.png
explanation: `-S` sorts largest first, and `-r` reverses that, so the smallest file comes first.

stem: Mira runs `ls -lt` and sees the most recently modified file at the top. Which option, added to the command, shows files by their last access time instead?

options.text: `-c`, which would sort by the status-change time
options.rationale: `-c` uses the time of the last status (inode) change, not the access time.
`-S` replaces the time sort with a size sort.
Correct: with `-t`, `-u` sorts by access time instead of modification time.
`-X` sorts by extension and has nothing to do with times.

explanation: `-t` sorts by time. By default that is the modification time; `-u` selects access time and `-c` the status-change time.

stem: What does the `-r` option do in `ls -lSr`?

options.rationale: That is `-R`, in capital letters.
Correct: `-r` reverses whichever order is in use.

options.text: It restricts the listing to regular files
options.rationale: `ls` has no such option; `find -type f` would do that.

options.text: It removes the entries it lists
options.rationale: `ls` never deletes anything.

explanation: Lower-case `-r` reverses the order; upper-case `-R` recurses. Mixing up that pair is a common slip.

stem: In the output of `ls -l`, which column comes right after the owner and the group?

options.rationale: Correct: after the owner and group come the size, then the date and time, then the name.
The link count sits before the owner, right after the permissions.
The name is the last column.
The permissions are the first column.

explanation: A long listing reads: type and permissions, link count, owner, group, size, date and time, name.

stem: Jonas has a file called `boss fight.ogg`. Which command removes exactly that file?

options.rationale: The shell passes two names, `boss` and `fight.ogg`.
A plus sign doesn't stand for a space in a file name.
Correct: the quotes keep the space inside one argument.
That names a different file.

explanation: Quotes or a backslash before the space (`boss\ fight.ogg`) make the shell treat the name as one word.

stem: The release folder holds `level1.txt`, `level2.txt` and `level10.txt`. Which `find` command lists only the first two?

options.rationale: Correct: `?` matches exactly one character.
`*` also matches `10`, so all three would be listed.
This needs exactly two characters and lists only `level10.txt`.
`-type` takes a one-letter type such as `f` or `d`, not a name.

explanation: In `find -name`, as in shell globbing, `?` stands for one character and `*` for any number of characters, including none. Quote the pattern so `find` sees it.

stem: With `ls -lh`, what does a size shown as `4.0K` mean?

options.rationale: Correct: `K` stands for kilobytes (units of 1024 bytes).

options.text: 4 kilobits per second, a transfer speed
options.rationale: `ls` shows file sizes, not speeds.

options.text: The file has 4 links and a `K` permission
options.rationale: Links and permissions are separate columns.
Sizes are in bytes, scaled with a unit letter by `-h`.

explanation: `-h` scales sizes to `K`, `M` or `G`. Without it, the size is given in bytes.
